titre: “Wherefore Art Thou Romeo?”: Juliet Is Not Looking for Romeo
accroche: In the balcony scene, Juliet is not asking where Romeo is: “wherefore” means “why,” and her next lines say so.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Romeo, Romeo, where are you?” That is how the most famous line of *Romeo and Juliet* is commonly read. The misreading comes from one word: *wherefore*, which looks like *where* but means “why.”

## What the Text Says

Act 2, scene 2. Juliet, on the balcony, does not know that Romeo is listening in the garden. She says: “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”, then, right away: “Deny thy father and refuse thy name.” In other words: disown your father, give up your name. Further on in the same speech, she concludes: “Thou art thyself, though not a Montague.” You are you, even without being a Montague.

The context leaves no ambiguity: Juliet is not asking where Romeo is (she does not know he is there), but why he is Romeo, that is, why he bears the name of the enemy family.

## A Vanished Word

In modern English, *wherefore* is archaic: the dictionary defines it as “why, for what reason.” It barely survives except through this line, and that is what makes it deceptive: a forgotten word, which looks like a common word, reads as a question of place.

## The Rest of the Speech

Shakespeare's text itself develops the idea. Juliet goes on: “'Tis but thy name that is my enemy” (only your name is my enemy), then asks: “What's Montague?” It is, she says, neither a hand, nor a foot, nor an arm, nor a face, nor any other part belonging to a man. Then comes the famous image of the rose, which would smell as sweet under another name, and the request to strip himself of that name: “Romeo, doff thy name.” Romeo, who had not planned to speak up, replies: “I take thee at thy word,” and swears that he will never again be Romeo. He adds that his name is hateful to him “because it is an enemy to you”: the name is the subject of the scene from beginning to end.

## What It Shifts

The misreading does not change just a word: it changes the scene. Juliet is not searching for a lover: she is arguing against a name, and the scene that is played as a game of hide-and-seek is a piece of reasoning about what a name adds, or does not add, to a person.

carte.punch: “Wherefore art thou Romeo?”: Juliet is not asking where Romeo is.
carte.idee: In 16th-century English, “wherefore” means “why.” Juliet is asking why Romeo bears the name of the enemy family, as the next line shows: “Deny thy father and refuse thy name.”

quiz.question: What is Juliet asking when she says “wherefore art thou Romeo?”
choix: Where Romeo is hiding in the Capulets' garden
Why he bears the name of the enemy family
How Romeo managed to get into the Capulets' garden
When Romeo will finally come to meet her
quiz.explication: “Wherefore” means “why.” The next line (“Deny thy father and refuse thy name”) shows that she is talking about the name, not the place.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which line of Juliet's speech confirms the meaning of “wherefore”?
choix: “Deny thy father and refuse thy name”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The line immediately after asks Romeo to disown his name: the question was about his name, not his whereabouts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Romeo reply after hearing Juliet's reasoning about his name?
choix: He warns her that he is about to make himself known to her
He swears never again to be called Romeo, “I take thee at thy word”
He asks her not to disown her own name
He leaves the garden without being seen
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Romeo replies “I take thee at thy word” and swears never again to be Romeo, since that name has become an enemy to her.
